note: Key sites of the divided kingdom and the journeys of Elijah & Elisha. x/y are PERCENT positions on israel-judah-split-map.jpg (placed on each city's dot, clear of its printed label). cat: calf | capital | prophet | event. holy = verified holylandsite.com article link (omit if none). Each blurb opens with the site's origin/pre-history, then its divided-kingdom significance.

sites.name: Damascus
sites.blurb: One of the world's oldest cities — Abraham's steward Eliezer came from here — and by these centuries the capital of Aram, Israel's fiercest northern enemy. Elisha healed the Syrian general Naaman of his leprosy; and, sent to anoint Hazael king, Elisha wept, foreseeing the cruelty Hazael would one day inflict on Israel.

sites.name: Zarephath (by Sidon)
sites.blurb: A town of Sidon — Phoenicia's oldest port, named for Canaan's firstborn son. Here, in the famine, Elijah was fed by a Gentile widow: her meal and oil multiplied, her dead son raised. Jesus cited it at Nazareth as proof that God's mercy crosses borders.

sites.name: Tyre
sites.blurb: Phoenicia's great island fortress-port, tied to Israel twice over. Its King Hiram supplied the cedar and gold — and the master bronze-worker (also named Hiram) — for Solomon's temple. Yet a few reigns later Tyre sent Israel a darker gift: its princess Jezebel, who married Ahab and brought the Baal cult, and its prophets, into the heart of the North.

sites.name: Dan
sites.blurb: Originally the Canaanite town of Laish, seized and renamed by the tribe of Dan — who set up their own graven image and priesthood here, centuries before Jeroboam chose the very same spot for a golden calf. The northern point of 'from Dan to Beersheba'; its high-place platform has been excavated.

sites.name: Mt Carmel
sites.blurb: Carmel means 'God's orchard' — a lush ridge, a fitting stage for the contest over who truly sends the rain. Here Elijah faced 450 prophets of Baal: the God who answers by fire is God. The fire fell — and then, after three rainless years, the sky went black and the rain returned.

sites.name: Jezreel
sites.blurb: In the fertile Jezreel Valley — the name means 'God sows' — stood Ahab and Jezebel's northern palace, and here their dynasty was destroyed. Ahab had Naboth murdered here to seize his vineyard, and Elijah foretold the ruin of Ahab's house. Years later the army commander Jehu made it happen: in a single day at Jezreel he killed Joram (Ahab's son, king of Israel) and Ahaziah (king of Judah — Ahab's grandson through his daughter Athaliah), and had Jezebel thrown from a window to her death. Ahab's line fell here, in both kingdoms at once.

sites.name: Shunem
sites.blurb: A village in the Jezreel Valley, home of the wealthy 'Shunammite woman' who built a room on her roof for Elisha whenever he passed by. When her only son later died, Elisha came and raised him back to life — the mirror of Elijah's raising of the widow's son at Zarephath.

sites.name: Samaria
sites.blurb: Omri bought the hill of Shemer and named his new capital Samaria after him; Ahab adorned it with an ivory palace. Aram later besieged it until famine drove mothers to eat their children — until Elisha foretold deliverance overnight. In 722 BC it fell to Assyria, and the ten tribes were carried into exile.

sites.name: Shechem
sites.blurb: An ancient covenant center — which is exactly why the tribes gathered here to make a king. Abraham built his first altar in the promised land at Shechem, and Joseph was buried here; and between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, which flank the town, Joshua gathered all Israel to renew the covenant — 'choose you this day whom ye will serve.' As the traditional place where the northern tribes ratified kingship, this is where all Israel came to crown Rehoboam. When he answered harshly, the ten tribes broke away, and Jeroboam made Shechem his first capital. The place of covenant-making had become the place of the split.

sites.name: Bethel
sites.blurb: Named by Jacob after his dream of a ladder to heaven — 'this is none other but the house of God.' Bethel means 'House of God' (the town was once called Luz). The bitter irony: Jeroboam set a golden calf in the very 'House of God' — the southern of his two shrines, near the Judah border, meant to keep the North from going up to Jerusalem. Here too a company of prophets lived, and the youths who mocked Elisha met the two bears.

sites.name: Jericho & the Jordan
sites.blurb: Jericho, the 'city of palms,' was the first city Israel took — its walls falling at the trumpet blast — and the Jordan beside it is where the nation first crossed into the land. Here Elijah parted the waters and was taken up in a chariot of fire; Elisha caught his mantle and healed Jericho's poisoned spring; and in this river Naaman washed seven times and was cleansed.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.blurb: Older than the kingdom itself — Salem of Melchizedek, Mount Moriah where Abraham bound Isaac, the Jebusite fortress David took for his capital, and the hill where Solomon built the temple. In the Deuteronomist's vision this was the one place worship rightly belonged — the sanctuary Jeroboam's calves were built to rival. The reforming kings Hezekiah and Josiah fought to enforce it, tearing down the rival high places and gathering all worship here. In 586 BC the city and its temple finally fell to Babylon.

sites.name: Mount Horeb (Sinai)
sites.blurb: The mountain of Moses — where God met him in the burning bush and gave Israel the law — far to the south, beyond the edge of this map. Fleeing Jezebel after Carmel, Elijah walked forty days to Horeb, and there the LORD passed by: not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in a still small voice.
